objects.name: CTFT Project
objects.description: Capture-The-Flag Techniques - an ontology of CTF solving behaviour. Relates to MITRE ATT&CK, CAPEC and CWE as per-entry anchors; not a parallel ATT&CK. Generalized from FOM.

objects.name: Cryptography
objects.description: Deliberately weakened or layered crypto and its cryptanalysis. (HTB: Crypto)

objects.name: CTFTTE-CRY-001 - Weak RSA parameter design
objects.description: The author ships RSA with an exploitable weakness: tiny e, close primes, shared modulus, or partial key leakage.

objects.name: CTFTCTE-CRY-001 - Recover the RSA private key from weak parameters
objects.description: Identify the weakness class and apply the matching attack (Fermat, Wiener, common-modulus, Coppersmith).
Counter-technique recovers/defeats the paired design technique. `mitigates` is kept for STIX-consumer compatibility; the CTFT semantics are carried by x_ctft_relation.

objects.name: CTFTTE-CRY-002 - Classical cipher layering

objects.name: CTFTCTE-CRY-002 - Break layered classical ciphers

objects.name: CTFTCTE-CRY-003 - Exploit key reuse and block-mode patterns

Counter-technique recovers/defeats the paired design technique. `mitigates` is kept for STIX-consumer compatibility; the CTFT semantics are carried by x_ctft_relation.

objects.name: CTFTTE-CRY-012 - Hash-cracking maze with constraints
objects.description: The flag is a hash whose preimage satisfies extra constraints (mask, salt, charset). The hash itself is strong (sha256crypt and peers), so raw brute force is hopeless; the intended path is that the shape of the plaintext is leaked by the challenge story and the solver must turn that shape into a mask or rule set. A second, harder variant gives a plaintext that follows an external fixed format — a word address, a date, a serial number — where each position's character class is known, collapsing the keyspace by orders of magnitude. The concealment is the missing constraint statement: the solver must notice that the format is knowable before any attack can succeed.

objects.name: CTFTCTE-CRY-012 - Crack hashes under masks/rules
objects.description: Identify the hash type, build masks/rules, crack with hashcat/john, and verify. When the plaintext follows a known external format (word address, date, serial), derive the mask position-by-position from that format — custom charsets per position — before spending GPU time; a format-constrained mask collapses the keyspace far below any wordlist.
Counter-technique recovers/defeats the paired design technique. `mitigates` is kept for STIX-consumer compatibility; the CTFT semantics are carried by x_ctft_relation.

objects.name: CTFTTE-CRY-013 - Nonstandard-alphabet substitution (braille, cetacean)
objects.description: The flag is encoded in a nonstandard alphabet: Braille, cetacean/whale-speak, or a custom substitution.

objects.name: CTFTCTE-CRY-013 - Transcode nonstandard alphabets

objects.name: CTFTTE-CRY-014 - Timestamp-keyed XOR
objects.description: The ciphertext is a plain repeating-key XOR, but the key is stored nowhere: it is the decimal string of the epoch timestamp at which the writer touched the file (e.g. str(time.Now().Unix())). Generic decoders fail because the key looks like arbitrary digits with unknown provenance. The trap is that the key is leaked by the filesystem itself — the file's last-modification time. A twist: a guardian process may re-encrypt on every read, so the mtime of the last write, not the original one, is the one that matches the final ciphertext.

objects.name: CTFTCTE-CRY-014 - Derive the XOR key from file mtime
objects.description: 1. Read the file's last-modification time with full precision (stat, date -r, or os.stat().stmtime). 2. Convert to epoch seconds and use the decimal string as the repeating XOR key over the hex-decoded ciphertext. 3. If the mtime was disturbed (guardian still running, tool re-writing the file), sweep a ±N-second window around plausible write times and score each candidate key by printable ASCII ratio or a flag-format regex. 4. Beware timezone and truncation variants: try local vs UTC parsing, integer vs sub-second float, and RFC3339-formatted strings as alternative key spellings.
Counter-technique recovers/defeats the paired design technique. `mitigates` is kept for STIX-consumer compatibility; the CTFT semantics are carried by x_ctft_relation.

objects.name: CTFTTE-CRY-015 - RSA exponent bound by a small linear relation
objects.description: Nothing looks weak: N = p·q is a healthy balanced semiprime, e is full-size, no prime, no bit of d and no helper value is leaked. What is small is not the private exponent but a linear relation the public exponent satisfies: $$e\,x + y \equiv 0 \pmod{\varphi(N)}, \qquad x \approx N^{1/4}, \quad |y| \approx N^{1/8}$$ Every textbook test fails. d is full size, so Wiener (d < N^{1/4}/3) and Boneh-Durfee (d < N^{0.292}) return nothing, Fermat/Pollard never apply, and RsaCtfTool reports "no attack succeeded" because none of its modules test a bounded (x, y) relation. The trap is that the weakness lives in the shape of the exponent pair, invisible to a scanner looking at d alone. The canonical generator is the Yen-Kim-Lim-Moon exponentiation scheme, published as a countermeasure to CRT fault attacks. With φ = φ(N) and a quarter-size bound B = 2^{nbits/4}: er, r ← [1, B] # two small secrets dr = er⁻¹ mod φ d = dr + r # full-size "perturbed" private exponent e = d⁻¹ mod φ # full-size public exponent d is dr plus a 256-bit noise, so it never enters a small-d window. Multiplying e·(dr + r) ≡ 1 by er collapses the construction into the relation above: $$e\,\underbrace{(1 + er r)}{x \approx N^{1/4}} \;\underbrace{- er}{y \approx N^{1/8}} \equiv 0 \pmod{\varphi(N)}$$ Two publication variants: - Parameters published. er and r are printed next to N, e, c. The relation is then immediately evaluable: kφ(N) = e(1 + er·r) − er is a multiple of the totient, and d ≡ e⁻¹ (mod kφ(N)) decrypts — a multiple of φ is as good as φ itself. - Parameters withheld. Only N, e, c are given. The bounded relation is the sole residue of the construction, and it is exactly the input of the generalized Wiener attack (Nitaj, PKC 2004), whose Theorem 2 asks for x ≤ ⅓N^{1/4} and |y| ≤ ½cN^{−3/4}ex with c ≤ 1 — satisfied here because er, r = O(N^{1/8}). The same smell appears whenever an author "adds noise" to a modular inverse instead of drawing d fresh, or reuses one small multiplier across several keys: any leak of x (or of a multiple of φ, see CTFTCTE-CRY-001) plus a small y reopens this relation.

objects.name: CTFTCTE-CRY-015 - Recover the factors from a bounded exponent relation
objects.description: Given N, e (and c), recover φ(N) — or the factors — from e·x + y ≡ 0 (mod φ) with small x, y. Two branches, cheapest first. Branch A — the small parameters are published (er, r given). Evaluate the relation directly; it is a multiple of the totient, and a multiple of φ is enough: kphi = e (1 + er r) - er # == k φ(N) d = inverse(e, kphi) # valid mod kφ, hence mod φ m = pow(c, d, N) Validate with pow(m, e, N) == c, never with the flag format alone. Branch B — only N, e, c are published (generalized Wiener). x sits at the edge of the convergent denominators of e/N, so continued fractions enumerate it: 1. Compute the convergents of e/N — and, when they do not close, their semiconvergents (h{i-1} + j·h{i-2}) / (k{i-1} + j·k{i-2}), because x sits between two convergents as soon as it nears the N^{1/4} edge of the window. 2. For each candidate k/x, s = N + 1 − ⌊e·x / k⌋ estimates p + q; t = s² − 4N estimates (p − q)². 3. If t is a perfect square (search a ±2 window around s to absorb the flooring error), then p = (s + t^{1/2})/2 and N mod p == 0 closes the branch. 4. Otherwise p̃ = (s + ⌊t^{1/2}⌋)/2 is within N^{1/4} of the true prime: Coppersmith f(X) = p̃ + X with X = N^{1/4}, plus the small shifts (2j+1)·N^{1/4} that recentre the unknown, and keep any root that divides N. 5. d = e⁻¹ mod φ, decrypt, re-encrypt to confirm. Expected cost: milliseconds for branch A, under a second for branch B on replayed instances of this construction. The fraction sweep — convergents first, then their semiconvergents — closes roughly nine instances out of ten directly. The residual failures are exactly the instances where x > N^{1/4}/3, i.e. where the theorem's own hypothesis fails: past that edge neither the fraction sweep nor the p̃ + X route is guaranteed, and the next move is a bivariate lattice on the relation itself. Do not read the fallback as dead code. What fails and must not be retried. Wiener (d is full size), Boneh-Durfee (d > N^{0.292}), Fermat (primes are independent and balanced), Pollard p−1, and every automated sweep that only looks at d. Recognising that the weakness is in (x, y), not in d, is the whole solve.
Counter-technique recovers/defeats the paired design technique. `mitigates` is kept for STIX-consumer compatibility; the CTFT semantics are carried by x_ctft_relation.
